texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Q: Should I always run an experiment when I make a change to my product? If not, when should I not?
texts.text: Q: Should I always run an experiment when I make a change to my product? If not, when should I not?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If you work at a large company, every change you make is likely run as an experiment – partly because you need to demonstrate your impact, and partly because even small changes can have large unintended consequences.
texts.text: If you work at a large company, every change you make is likely run as an experiment – partly because you need to demonstrate your impact, and partly because even small changes can have large unintended consequences.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If you work at a small startup, nothing is run as an experiment because there just isn’t enough data.
texts.text: If you work at a small startup, nothing is run as an experiment because there just isn’t enough data.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: So this question is really for people who work at companies in that in-between phase. Which happens to be most companies.
texts.text: So this question is really for people who work at companies in that in-between phase. Which happens to be most companies.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Let’s first talk about why experiments are valuable, the downside of running experiments, and finally when to NOT run an experiment.
texts.text: Let’s first talk about why experiments are valuable, the downside of running experiments, and finally when to NOT run an experiment.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Why run an experiment at all?
texts.text: Why run an experiment at all?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It’s easy to take this for granted, but the fact that you can know the precise impact of your changes is…incredible. Who outside of the software space is able to tell if a change they made in language, color, or user experience is definitively helping or hurting their business? It’s amazing.
texts.text: It’s easy to take this for granted, but the fact that you can know the precise impact of your changes is…incredible. Who outside of the software space is able to tell if a change they made in language, color, or user experience is definitively helping or hurting their business? It’s amazing.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: More broadly, the benefits of running your changes as an experiment are many:
texts.text: More broadly, the benefits of running your changes as an experiment are many:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: : Experiments help you learn about your users
texts.text: : Experiments help you learn about your users

texts.label: text
texts.orig: : Experiments tell you if your change had the intended consequence
texts.text: : Experiments tell you if your change had the intended consequence

texts.label: text
texts.orig: : Experiments precisely quantify the impact of your changes (and your team)
texts.text: : Experiments precisely quantify the impact of your changes (and your team)

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: What are the downsides of running an experiment?
texts.text: What are the downsides of running an experiment?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: : Experiments take time to set up and run
texts.text: : Experiments take time to set up and run

texts.label: text
texts.orig: : Experiments can create false confidence based on misinterpreted results
texts.text: : Experiments can create false confidence based on misinterpreted results

texts.label: text
texts.orig: : Experiments can push you to think short-term
texts.text: : Experiments can push you to think short-term

texts.label: text
texts.orig: : Experiments disincentivize taking bets that are hard to measure
texts.text: : Experiments disincentivize taking bets that are hard to measure

texts.label: text
texts.orig: : Experiments can introduce awkward user-experiences or legal risk
texts.text: : Experiments can introduce awkward user-experiences or legal risk

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: When should you NOT run an experiment?
texts.text: When should you NOT run an experiment?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In spite of the downsides, I’m a big fan of experiments and generally default to running every change through an experiment. But, there are three cases where you should probably skip the experiment and just ship the change:
texts.text: In spite of the downsides, I’m a big fan of experiments and generally default to running every change through an experiment. But, there are three cases where you should probably skip the experiment and just ship the change:

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 1. It’ll take too long to get actionable results
texts.text: 1. It’ll take too long to get actionable results

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This is by far the main reason to skip running an experiment, and in my experience still far too underappreciated. Until you are at significant scale, experiments probably aren’t even worth thinking about. Particularly on features buried within your product.
texts.text: This is by far the main reason to skip running an experiment, and in my experience still far too underappreciated. Until you are at significant scale, experiments probably aren’t even worth thinking about. Particularly on features buried within your product.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Let’s take an example: Say you wanted to measure the conversion impact of a copy change on the last step of your sign-up flow, which is currently converting at 10%.
texts.text: Let’s take an example: Say you wanted to measure the conversion impact of a copy change on the last step of your sign-up flow, which is currently converting at 10%.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: How many users would need to go through this step in order for you to notice a 5% change in conversion?
texts.text: How many users would need to go through this step in order for you to notice a 5% change in conversion?

texts.orig: Furthermore, if you are looking to see the impact on your brand, network effects, long-term retention, or anything else that takes months/years to notice, you also shouldn’t wait for an experiment to run its course before making a call. Consider just launching it and keeping a small holdout to measure the long-term impact.
texts.text: Furthermore, if you are looking to see the impact on your brand, network effects, long-term retention, or anything else that takes months/years to notice, you also shouldn’t wait for an experiment to run its course before making a call. Consider just launching it and keeping a small holdout to measure the long-term impact.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The second most common reason to skip running an experiment is a low risk/reward ratio. Before running an experiment, answer these questions:
texts.text: The second most common reason to skip running an experiment is a low risk/reward ratio. Before running an experiment, answer these questions:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Is your change a best practice and already worked well for others? (e.g. moving buttons above the fold, fewer steps in a flow, making your pitch clearer, etc.)
texts.text: Is your change a best practice and already worked well for others? (e.g. moving buttons above the fold, fewer steps in a flow, making your pitch clearer, etc.)

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Will you be able to detect significant negative impact in other ways? (e.g. before/after data, CX)
texts.text: Will you be able to detect significant negative impact in other ways? (e.g. before/after data, CX)

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: What’s the most negative impact you’ve ever seen from an experiment like this?
texts.text: What’s the most negative impact you’ve ever seen from an experiment like this?

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: What will you concretely do with experiment results once you have them?
texts.text: What will you concretely do with experiment results once you have them?

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: What’s been the typical time for your team to set-up and analyze experiments?
texts.text: What’s been the typical time for your team to set-up and analyze experiments?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Now you need to make a decision:
texts.text: Now you need to make a decision:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Making this change without an experiment, or taking your team’s time from higher-impact work?
texts.text: Making this change without an experiment, or taking your team’s time from higher-impact work?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If you can run experiments quickly and easily (e.g. a few hours), this decision is generally easy: run the experiment. If running experiments is a pain in the butt, and the changes are relatively benign, you can probably skip the experiment. If it’s somewhere in between, it’s a judgment call, but I personally default to running an experiment.
texts.text: If you can run experiments quickly and easily (e.g. a few hours), this decision is generally easy: run the experiment. If running experiments is a pain in the butt, and the changes are relatively benign, you can probably skip the experiment. If it’s somewhere in between, it’s a judgment call, but I personally default to running an experiment.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You may notice that the key variable in this formula is the time it takes to run and analyze experiments. The easier that process is, the more often you’ll end up running experiments, and the more you’ll learn. So if anything, spend time making that process easier.

texts.orig: As your company grows, and your individual impact is judged based on quantifiable results from experiments, skipping experiments becomes tougher. That’s normal. Still, no matter what stage your company is at, I hope these examples give your team some direction the next time you face this question.
